title: Damien Aubin Documents a Former Soviet Mining Settlement Suspended in Time
description: The small settlement of Pyramiden on the Norwegian archipelago of Svalbard is literally frozen in time. A former mining outpost for the Soviet Uni
body:
The small settlement of Pyramiden on the Norwegian archipelago of Svalbard is literally frozen in time. A former mining outpost for the Soviet Union, industrial operations ceased in 1998, and residents relocated. It wasn’t until 2007 that a handful of new inhabitants made the settlement home.
Because Pyramiden was abandoned in a cold climate, it remains impeccably preserved, with remnants of its once-thriving settlement still visible. French photographer Damien Aubin visited the Arctic region and documented the still, serene environment blanketed in snow. “The place has not been abandoned. It has been left in suspension,” he says. 
Classroom, Pyramiden
Pyramiden’s buildings and the objects inside are largely unchanged. Books sit open on school desks, and an unblemished statue of Lenin presides over a common area. Outside, a towering outdoor monument soars into the sky, the vibrant red and blue paint a stark contrast to the otherwise white landscape. 
“I photograph these environments at a distance, in a restrained, diffuse light. There is no event to describe, no narrative to unfold,” Aubin adds. “Across Pyramiden, Barentsburg and Longyearbyen, the same condition appears:spaces shaped by human intent, no longer aligned with it.”
Aubin has compiled the photos in a limited-edition book slated for release in September. You can purchase a copy on his website.

title: Felicia Chiao's Domestic Scenes Reflect the Emotional Structures of Daily Life
description: “When I was really little, I wanted to be one of those stackable chairs you’d see in like a school auditorium,” Felicia Chiao says. “I thought the
body:
“When I was really little, I wanted to be one of those stackable chairs you’d see in like a school auditorium,” Felicia Chiao says. “I thought they looked cozy.” This childhood memory is the basis for a playful drawing in which Chiao’s signature characters mound atop one another. Layering reigns in this imagined world as calendars and clocks emerge from the wall in dense piles, while stacks of books and dishes rest on the floor. 
Chiao is known for her warm illustrations that capture emotion and the variances of mental health through surreal, flower-filled scenes. Working in pencil, ink, and watercolor, the artist renders compositions that feel both timeless and indicative of our current age, in which the anxieties and tribulations of life today emerge through curious characters.
“Stacks”
Alongside her largely domestic scenes, Chiao has also been adding to her growing collection of Lunar New Year drawings, which feature the animal of the year set against a gilded and crimson backdrop. 
Play and constraint also figure prominently into the artist’s approach. “I did a very cool collaboration with Heath Ceramics last year, and while it was a completely different medium than what I am used to, I think it has influenced my drawing process,” she says. “I’ve been experimenting with more mixed media (watercolor, color pencil, markers, sometimes a little gouache or gel pen).” The mats for frames are similar, as she enjoys the challenge of customizing the otherwise stark white material to complement her works.
This October, Chiao will open a solo show with Harman Projects and has several exhibitions slated for the coming years. She offers a variety of prints through her shop, and you can keep up with her latest works and collaborations on Instagram.

title: A New Colossal Shop Collection Highlights Local Artists and Chicago-Made Goods
description: Colossal has always called Chicago home. We love highlighting artists and designers in our own community, and the Colossal Shop’s newest collectio
body:
Colossal has always called Chicago home. We love highlighting artists and designers in our own community, and the Colossal Shop’s newest collection brings our creative neighbors to a wider global audience.
This selection features one-of-a-kind and handmade objects from Chicago-based artists we’re excited to share a city with. From unique ceramic forms to thoughtfully designed apparel, there’s something exciting for everyone.
Shop the collection now.

Periwinkle Ripple Mugs
With rhythmic, stacked silhouettes and looping handles, these one-of-a-kind mugs turn morning coffees into a sculptural experience. Created as a series of 8 exclusively for Colossal, each retro-futuristic mug is uniquely hand-thrown and assembled by Chicago ceramic artist Dara Schuman. Read more about her work here.




The Kami Bag
A chic reinterpretation of the quintessential brown paper grocery bag, the Kami Bag designed by Bukuro is handcrafted from richly textured leather and lined in a soft suede. Both a unique accessory and fascinating conversation piece, its familiar form is elevated through thoughtful construction and unexpected materials.




Miniature Ceramic Animals
Starting Projects creates the cutest, tiniest friends to keep you company. Adopt a creature to roam your desk, bookshelf, or trinket display. Or, surprise a loved one with a miniature version of their pet. We currently have eight breeds to choose from.




Seed Libraries and Agave Grow Kits
Immerse yourself in a new tale of growing your own herbs, vegetables, and desert plants inside your own abode. Founded by two regular thumb-colored people inside their Chicago home, Modern Sprout makes thoughtfully crafted products to simplify plants and indoor gardening.




Hats and Helping Hand Trays
What better way to express your enthusiasm for hats and dogs? Chicago-based artist Joe Kraft works with a variety of materials. While exploring ceramics, the artist creates design objects like the Helping Hand Tray—your daily dish for keys, rings, cash, and more. However, his love for drawing and printmaking drives his practice, which informs his line of apparel, including bright, fun dad caps.




Magic Wand Spoons and Swirl Star Incense Holders
Hand-built one at a time, these stoneware pieces are small but mighty. DAiLY SPECiAL—a small ceramics studio by multidisciplinary artist Lulu Luyao Chang—creates whimsical hand-built ceramics, jewelry, cups, and home goods that blend playful nostalgia with organic forms.




Emerging Artist Hats and Kiln Loader Totes
Artist and illustrator Molly Anne Bishop is inspired by nature, the mundane, and the boring, everyday things we all have to do. If you’ve ever loaded a kiln, you can probably relate to this awkward, quirky, puzzle-like process. And the Emerging Artist hat is a celebration of the potential inside of all of us and a tribute to our local cicada friends popping up to visit.



Silver Accessories
Why settle for plain hairstyles and ordinary lighters? Yard Sale Jewelry is the world of Ali Romero, a Chicago-based metals artist connected to organic forms and driven by a passion for transformation and natural elements.



Risograph Printed Matchboxes
Add some charm to your living room, kitchen, or bedside table. These small-batch risograph-printed matchboxes by Sunroom don playful illustrations of vibrant butterflies, cozy summer campfires, and striped edges, turning an everyday essential into a whimsical experience.
Find the full collection in the Colossal Shop.

title: Nvidia CEO Pours $75M Into San Francisco Art Campus
description:
News
                Vanderbilt University's building on the ruins of the California College of the Arts will bear the billionai
body:
News
                Vanderbilt University's building on the ruins of the California College of the Arts will bear the billionaire's name   
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang on January 5, 2026 (photo Patrick T. Fallon/AFP via Getty Images)
    
        
            Vanderbilt University's new San Francisco arts and design campus will bear the name of Nvidia co-founder Jensen (Jen-Hsun) Huang after the billionaire committed millions to the institution. The university announced this week that the AI chipmaker and his wife, Lori Huang, gifted $75 million to establish the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang College of Art, Architecture and Design.The controversial campus will replace the nearly 120-year-old California College of the Arts (CCA), San Francisco's last remaining private art school. The beloved nonprofit institution, which grants bachelor's and master's degrees across artistic disciplines, was purchased by Vanderbilt amid financial struggles caused by a decline in enrollment and a growing budget deficit.The Huangs donated a $22.5 million matching gift to CCA in February 2025 to help stabilize the institution's shaky finances. However, not even a full year later, CCA announced that it would cease operating after the 2026–2027 academic year, and that the Potrero Hill campus would be subsumed by Vanderbilt. Not everyone in the local art community is happy with Huang's donation. "These billionaires would much rather play God and remake our art schools in their own image than support a 120-year-old legacy fine art school," Lindsey White, a San Francisco-based artist, educator, and CCA alum, told Hyperallergic."In both CCA and SFAI cases, billionaires with zero experience in the arts have taken over major real estate, leaving local artists, educators, and workers in a dystopian nightmare," White continued. "Sadly, it seems our local government didn't see the value in saving the last fine art school in Northern California either."California Governor Gavin Newsom had worked to secure a $20 million public grant in 2025 to keep the private institution afloat despite significant opposition from state lawmakers. At the time, the governor argued that though it was atypical for the government to fund a private college, the state should fund CCA to safeguard its cultural sector amid Trump's attacks on the arts. He later expressed shock at the school's closure, but critics said he should've seen it coming. Huang co-founded Nvidia, a manufacturer of graphics processing units (GPUs) now widely used to power artificial intelligence programs, in a Denny's restaurant booth in 1993. In May, the chipmaker reached a valuation of $5.5 trillion, the highest in the history of publicly traded companies. According to the university's announcement, the Huangs donated the large sum out of their belief that "creative practice [is] one of innovation’s most essential engines."“Technology expands what we can build," Jensen Huang said in the press release issued earlier this week. "Art and design determine why we build it. Together they shape civilization."In an op-ed about the closure of CCA in the San Francisco Chronicle earlier this year, local gallerist Griff Williams warned that "corporate interests seem to eclipse all else in San Francisco.""Mayor Lurie, the closure of the California College of the Arts is a tragedy for the city, not a 'win,'" he wrote. "It’s another blow to the legacy of the heroes who made San Francisco unique: Joan Brown, David Ireland, Bruce Conner, Hung Liu, Hank Willis Thomas, Dewey Crumpler, Robert Arneson, Manuel Neri, Harrell Fletcher, Jim Goldberg, Viola Frey, Ted Purves, Dodie Bellamy and Susan O’Malley, to name a few."

title: A View From the Easel
description:
Community
                “Always in stock: coffee, beer, tequila, and that Swiss chocolate named Ragusa.”
body:
Community
                “Always in stock: coffee, beer, tequila, and that Swiss chocolate named Ragusa.”
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            Welcome to the 347th installment of A View From the Easel, a series in which artists reflect on their workspace. This week, Shahryar Nashat sculpts along to the sounds of Kelis's "Milkshake" and experiments with "a nautical glue the color of honey."Want to take part? Check out our submission guidelines and share a bit about your studio with us through this form! All mediums and workspaces are welcome, including your home studio.Shahryar Nashat, Asnières-sur-Seine, FranceHow long have you been working in this space?Three years this September. Although the space is similar to my former studio in Glendale, California, the journey couldn’t be different. Before, I drove by car through Laurel Canyon to the 101, then east on the 134 into Glendale. By the time you reached the studio, you’d already passed through a few different versions of Los Angeles. Here in Paris, it’s two wheels from the 11th, heading north through the 18th via République, watching the city thin out until you cross the Seine. Asnières-sur-Seine, just north of Paris, is also home to one of the first pet cemeteries in the world: le Cimetière des Chiens et Autres Animaux Domestiques.Describe an average day in your studio.Regular hours help structure the days and keep things moving when the direction of the work isn’t set yet. Always in stock: coffee, beer, tequila, and that Swiss chocolate named Ragusa (so close to a palindrome it hurts). Music is almost always on. Badalamenti’s Twin Peaks score only plays for difficult mold-making sessions. Lately it’s been ’90s: Erykah Badu, Lauryn Hill, Aaliyah, or Kelis. “I can teach you, but I have to charge.”How does the space affect your work?Making changes the work, but the inspiration never starts in the studio. The right tools, a good night’s sleep. That’s where it’s at. Light’s important too. This is what I miss from the West Coast days: the bright sunlight for forensic examinations and the roll-up gate. Scrolling it down was always a ritual, the sound of the day ending, whether it was a good one or if it all went to shite.How do you interact with the environment outside your studio?There are a handful of other artists in the building. All good people. My good friend Cooper Jacoby has a space here too. We have coffee and exchange notes on silicone cure times.What do you love about your studio?The proximity to Nouilles Fraîches Tibétaines on avenue Laurent Cély. The name speaks for itself. Fresh, homemade, and delicious. The same satisfaction as a burrito from El Sauz Tacos with Gabriel, at the corner of Chevy Chase and San Fernando Road.What do you wish were different?A little less warm in the summer, a little less cold in the winter.What is your favorite local museum?The Gustave Moreau Museum. Former studio, now museum, or mausoleum … all in one. This place is absurd. The main gallery is two stories tall with a massive skylight, and the walls are completely covered with paintings and drawings. It’s overwhelming in the best way. André Breton called it the most moving of all museums.What is your favorite art material to work with?Papier-mâché. A nautical glue the color of honey. More recently, Fabrican: a spray-on fabric that made its way down a bridal runway on Bella Hadid at Paris Haute Couture Fashion Week a couple years ago, and which I used to “dress” the Mothers sculptures currently on show at Gladstone on 64th Street in Manhattan. All are studio regulars. Oh, and anything acrylic by Golden.

title: Sable Elyse Smith Reveals the Shapes of State Violence
description:
Art Review
                The artist’s critique of the prison-industrial complex simultaneously deepens and skewers the legacie
body:
Art Review
                The artist’s critique of the prison-industrial complex simultaneously deepens and skewers the legacies of Minimalism.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            Sable Elyse Smith, “Coloring Book 111” (2022), screen printing ink, oil stick, and oil pastel on paper (all photos Liz Kim/Hyperallergic)AUSTIN — A sustained critique of the United States carceral system runs through Sable Elyse Smith's work. Clockwork at the Contemporary Austin, the culmination of her winning the 2026 Suzanne Deal Booth / FLAG Art Foundation Prize, consists mainly of paintings appropriating prison coloring books for visiting children on the first floor, and large-scale sculptures and installations on the second. Seen as a whole, Smith’s work co-opts Minimalism’s repetition and seriality as a metaphor for structural injustice, drawing attention to the rhythmic qualities of technological and administrative tyranny. The coloring books Smith adapts were originally created to help children emotionally absorb the violence of incarceration. Smith’s transformations seem to liquefact their pictures and texts so that they melt the foundations of the institutions they represent. Two works share the same page design, a waiting room of a courthouse filled with families as well as an assortment of creatures, asking — absurdly — “What 10 things don’t belong in this picture?” One version of Smith’s coloring scheme blocks in a select number of the human figures in solid blue, turning them into police officers as omnipotent institutional authority, while the other version places x’s and o’s across figures and faces, referencing the oppressiveness of such spaces. Smith rightly shifts the ludicrous question of belonging into a critique of recurrent power structures. Left: Sable Elyse Smith, “Coloring Book 117” (2023), screen printing ink, oil pastel, oil stick, and wax pencil on paper; right: Sable Elyse Smith, “BARRICADE” (2023), powder-coated aluminumSmith’s two videos fit like gloves together. “LAUGH TRACK, OR WHO’S THAT PEEKING IN MY WINDOW” (2021) is a series of footage appropriated from police reality TV shows, which are repeatedly rewound, fast-forwarded, and shown upside down. One sequence captures a routine traffic enforcement for a rolling stop that turns into a state-sanctioned detention without cause — under the pretense of an unrelated previous conviction, a police officer stops a vehicle and frisks its passenger, places him in cuffs, and takes pictures of his face and his back tattoos. A repeated xylophone noise draws attention to those moments when socially conditioned biases and bureaucratic procedures trigger state violence. Through the use of repetition in both footage and sound, Smith emphasizes the aggressive and senseless criminal profiling of an innocent person by juxtaposing Minimalism’s iterative assault against reality television’s numbing effects.In the adjacent “skin suit” (2025), law enforcement deals first with young White men. One sequence shows an officer finding drug and alcohol paraphernalia, along with a mask, a realistic pellet gun, gloves, and large knives contained in a bag in the trunk. After these extensive discoveries, the officer lets the person go, while giving him a fist bump. Afterward, another young White man is shown agitating an officer outside the open window of his patrol vehicle before the latter patiently drives away. This is juxtaposed with footage of a young Black man being held against his will due to the possession of marijuana. As the narrator later states, this video is about “bags of skin,” because “there are no people here” — the carceral system, Smith suggests, abstracts individuals entirely.  Smith’s sculptures are made of chairs and tables from prisons that are meant to be permanently drilled into the floor, rendered immovable like the institutions they represent. Their weaponization by the state is apparent in their rigidity, as tools that force imprisoned people into geometric configurations to better surveil them. This critique of the prison-industrial complex simultaneously deepens and skewers the legacies of Minimalism — one cannot help but think of Frank Stella’s polygons while surrounded by Smith’s work. Only, one also can’t help but notice the impotence of formal precision without larger social critique. Sable Elyse Smith, “BACKBEND” (2019), powder-coated aluminumSable Elyse Smith, “A Clockwork” (2021), aluminum, steel, and motorInstallation view of Sable Elyse Smith, “LAUGH TRACK, OR WHO’S THAT PEEKING IN MY WINDOW” (2021), high-definition video, color, and sound, 7:56 minutesInstallation view of Sable Elyse Smith: ClockworkSable Elyse Smith: Clockwork continues at the Contemporary Austin (3809 West 35th Street, Austin, Texas) through August 2. The exhibition was curated by Alex Klein and Julie Le. The exhibition will travel to the FLAG Art Foundation in New York in September; that iteration will be curated by Jonathan Rider.

title: Joyce Kozloff Reveals Herself as  Guerrilla Girls Founding Member
description:
News
                After decades of anonymity, the feminist artist and activist disclosed in an interview that she is the woman beh
body:
News
                After decades of anonymity, the feminist artist and activist disclosed in an interview that she is the woman behind the mask of “Liubov Popova.” 
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            Joyce Kozloff attends the opening reception for Local Editions: Prints by New York Artists (2018) at the Metropolitan Museum of Art (photo Taylor Hill via Getty Images)Artist and activist Joyce Kozloff has taken off the mask after 41 years, disclosing in a new interview with Art Journal Open that she was among the founding members of the Guerrilla Girls. She also revealed that “Liubov Popova” was her assigned pseudonym within the collective, whose members took the names of late women artists to maintain their own anonymity. In 2016, she published a (sneaky) biographical essay in Hyperallergic that both examined and lauded the Russian artist's creative evolution and career milestones throughout her unfortunately short life. “Remaining anonymous was an important Guerrilla Girls decision,” Kozloff explained to curators Maura Reilly and Helena Reckitt during her tell-all in the American magazine's Feminist Interview Project. “People thought this was to avoid art world reprisals. For me, that was never the reason. I argued for anonymity because I didn’t want attention to be on us as individuals, I wanted it to remain on the issues.”The artist said that she and two others were among the seven inaugural Guerrilla Girls who had lived through the women's movement in the 1970s, and that the younger women in the collective proclaimed that people had become disinterested with feminism, outlining a need for updated language and visuals. Having moved to Los Angeles when her husband Max began teaching at the California Institute of the Arts, Kozloff joined a feminist “consciousness raising” group that quickly radicalized her in 1971. This experience gave way to her role in co-organizing the Los Angeles Council of Women Artists (LACWA) that protested the paucity of female representation at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art.Kozloff's role in the feminist art movement expanded upon her return to New York in the early '70s — she was among the inaugural members of the Heresies Collective, and her art practice and shift to public art bolstered the emerging Pattern and Decoration movement.LACWA's data-driven protest model laid the basic framework for the Guerrilla Girls, which got its name after a new member misunderstood the title and brought a (now signature) gorilla mask to a meeting. Among the group's debut interventions was an ad campaign calling out the disparity between the number of women artists shown at the Metropolitan Museum of Art versus the number of displayed artworks depicting nude women.The group's confrontational wheat-pasted posters directly named and shamed institutions, galleries, and collectors that maintained sexist and racist hierarchies, drawing immense publicity and curiosity about the Guerrilla Girls' identities. “People were pissed and wanted to out us,” Kozloff told Reckitt and Reilly, adding that she was affiliated with the Guerrilla Girls until 1991. A printed reproduction of the Guerrilla Girls' “The Advantages of Being a Woman Artist” (1988) at the 2018 Gowanus Open Studios (photo Alissa Guzman/Hyperallergic)The artist also revealed her hand in developing one of the collective's most iconic poster campaigns — “The Advantages of Being a Woman Artist” (1988). She told Art Journal Open that the project was born from her time in a residency house she shared with married male artists who had brought their younger affair partners along as homemakers and unpaid studio assistants.“When I got back, I wrote a rough draft, 'The Disadvantages of Being a Woman Artist,'” Kozloff explained. “Until then, our posters always had verifiable statistics, so this was a stretch. But then, our clever members turned it around to 'Advantages,' and it worked!”Four decades on, Kozloff thinks that there has been enormous progress in the representation of women in the arts sphere. But, she said, “I'm very much more concerned about the current threats to women’s progress in the larger political realm,” citing the overturning of Roe v. Wade, the far-right push to keep women at home, and the beauty industry's invasive emphasis on youthful appearances.“But we can’t tell the next generation what to do, they will find their own ways,” she left off.
